nodes.summary: For triples of Booleans $b = (b_1, b_2, b_3)$ and $c = (c_1, c_2, c_3)$, the flags of the product are $(b_1 \land c_1,\ (b_2 \land c_1) \lor (b_1 \land c_2),\ (b_3 \land c_1) \lor (b_1 \land c_3))$.
nodes.title: Flags of a concatenation

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $k$, $i$ and $j$, the productions of a concatenation node $k$ with arguments $i$ and $j$ are the single production $k \to i\,j$ (nonterminal $i$ followed by nonterminal $j$) when $i < k$ and $j < k$, and there are none otherwise.
nodes.title: Productions of a concatenation node

nodes.summary: An encoded regular expression over an alphabet $\alpha$ is a list of regular-expression nodes, each a constant ($0$, $1$ or a letter) or an operator (sum, concatenation or star) whose arguments are node indices; the last node is the root. Any list is allowed: in the semantics, an argument that is not the index of an earlier node reads as $0$, and the empty list denotes $0$.
nodes.title: Encoded regular expressions

nodes.summary: Over a finite alphabet with decidable equality and a fixed enumeration of its letters, for all encoded regular expressions $e_1$ and $e_2$, the equivalence test returns true on $e_1$ and $e_2$ if and only if the regular expressions that $e_1$ and $e_2$ denote have the same language.
nodes.title: The equivalence test is correct

nodes.summary: Over a finite alphabet with decidable equality and a fixed enumeration of its letters, the equivalence test of two encoded regular expressions $e_1$ and $e_2$ returns true exactly when, for every length $n$ less than the search bound of $e_1$ and $e_2$ and every word $w$ of length $n$, the membership test gives the same answer for $e_1$ on $w$ as for $e_2$ on $w$.
nodes.title: Equivalence test

nodes.summary: For encoded regular expressions $e_1$ and $e_2$, the search bound is $2^{m + n}$, where $m$ and $n$ are the numbers of Thompson states of $e_1$ and $e_2$, each computed by one pass over the nodes of the encoding.
nodes.title: Search bound for equivalence

nodes.summary: The map sending an encoded regular expression over $\alpha$ to its list of nodes is a bijection onto the lists of regular-expression nodes over $\alpha$; its inverse wraps a list of nodes as an encoding.
nodes.title: Encodings are lists of nodes

nodes.summary: For a list $l$ of nodes and a natural number $k$, let $f_k$ be the entry at position $k$ of the flags of $l$, or the zero flags $(\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false})$ if $k$ is at least the length of $l$. Then $f_k$ describes the language of the regular expression at node $k$ of the encoding $l$ when $k$ is less than the length of $l$, and describes the empty language otherwise.
nodes.title: Correctness of the flag pass

nodes.summary: A triple of Booleans $(b_1, b_2, b_3)$ describes a language $L$ when $b_1$ is true exactly when $L$ is nonempty, $b_2$ is true exactly when $L$ contains a nonempty word, and $b_3$ is true exactly when $L$ is infinite.
nodes.title: Flags of a language

nodes.summary: For a list of nodes $n_0, \dots, n_{m-1}$, the flags $f_0, \dots, f_{m-1}$ are computed in one left-to-right pass: $f_k$ is the step flags of node $n_k$ computed from the flags $f_0, \dots, f_{k-1}$ of the nodes before it.
nodes.title: Flags of all nodes

nodes.summary: For a regular expression $r$ and a list $l$ of nodes, the nodes of $r$ are appended after $l$ in postorder, by recursion on $r$. For $0$, $1$ and a letter $a$, append the single node $0$, $1$ or $a$. For a sum $s + t$ (respectively a concatenation $st$), append the nodes of $s$ after $l$, giving $l_1$, then the nodes of $t$ after $l_1$, giving $l_2$, then a sum (respectively concatenation) node with arguments…
nodes.title: Postorder encoding after a prefix

nodes.summary: The encoding of a regular expression $r$ is the list of nodes obtained by appending the nodes of $r$ in postorder after the empty list, so that the root of $r$ is the last node.
nodes.title: Encoding of a regular expression

nodes.summary: For an encoded regular expression $e$, the language of a sentential form $X_1 \cdots X_n$ (terminals in $\alpha$, nonterminals in $\mathbb{N}$) is the product $L_1 \cdots L_n$, where $L_i$ is $\{a\}$, the language of the one-letter word $a$, when $X_i$ is the terminal $a$, and the language of the regular expression at node $k$ of $e$ when $X_i$ is the nonterminal $k$. The empty form has language $\{\varepsilon\}$.
nodes.title: Language of a sentential form

nodes.summary: For every list $l$ of nodes and every index $k$, the entry at index $k$ of the state counts of $l$ (read as $0$ past the end of the list) equals the Thompson state count of the regular expression at node $k$ of the encoding with nodes $l$ when $k$ is less than the length of $l$, and $0$ otherwise.
nodes.title: The pass computes the Thompson state count of every node

nodes.summary: Let $e$ be an encoded regular expression with nodes $n_0, \dots, n_{m-1}$, and let $f_0, \dots, f_{m-1}$ be the flags of all nodes of $e$, the triples of Booleans computed in one left-to-right pass over the nodes. The infiniteness test of $e$ is the third component of $f_{m-1}$, the flag triple of the last node (the root); when $e$ has no nodes it is false.
nodes.title: Infiniteness test for encoded regular expressions

nodes.summary: For an encoded regular expression $e$, the test returns the answer of the emptiness test for encoded context-free grammars on the grammar of $e$, which has one nonterminal per node and the root as start symbol.
nodes.title: Emptiness test for regular expressions

nodes.summary: For every encoded regular expression $e$, the language of the context-free grammar of $e$ (one nonterminal per node, the root as start symbol) equals the language of the regular expression that $e$ denotes.
nodes.title: The grammar generates the language of the expression

nodes.summary: For every list $l$ of nodes of encoded regular expressions, the list of state counts of $l$ has the same length as $l$.
nodes.title: One state count per node

nodes.summary: Let $e_1$ and $e_2$ be encoded regular expressions over an alphabet $\alpha$, and let $B$ be their search bound for equivalence. The regular expressions denoted by $e_1$ and $e_2$ match the same language if and only if every word $w$ over $\alpha$ of length less than $B$ is matched by the expression denoted by $e_1$ exactly when it is matched by the expression denoted by $e_2$.
nodes.title: Short distinguishing words for encoded regular expressions

nodes.summary: Two regular expressions $r$ and $s$ denote the same language if and only if every word of length less than $2^{n(r) + n(s)}$, where $n$ denotes the Thompson state count, is matched by $r$ exactly when it is matched by $s$.
nodes.title: Short distinguishing words

nodes.summary: For an encoded regular expression $e$ and a word $w$, the test returns the answer of the membership test for encoded context-free grammars on the word $w$ and the grammar of $e$, which has one nonterminal per node and the root as start symbol.
nodes.title: Membership test for regular expressions

nodes.summary: Let $e$ be an encoded regular expression. If a sentential form $u$ of the context-free grammar of $e$ yields a terminal word $w$, then $w$ belongs to the language of $u$: the concatenation, over the symbols of $u$, of $\{a\}$ for a terminal $a$ and of the language of the regular expression at node $k$ for a nonterminal $k$.
nodes.title: Soundness of the grammar of a regular expression

nodes.summary: Let $e$ be an encoded regular expression, $k$ a natural number and $x$ one of the productions of node $k$ built from the node of $e$ at index $k$. If a word $w$ belongs to the language of the right-hand side of $x$ (the concatenation, over its symbols, of $\{a\}$ for a terminal $a$ and of the language of the regular expression at node $i$ for a nonterminal $i$), then $w$ belongs to the language of the regular…
nodes.title: A production of a node only produces words of its language

nodes.summary: The bijection between the nodes of encoded regular expressions over $\alpha$ and $1 \oplus 1 \oplus \alpha \oplus (\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}) \oplus (\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}) \oplus \mathbb{N}$, where $1$ is the one-point type, that sends the zero node and the empty-word node to the first and second copies of $1$, a character node $a$ to $a$, a sum node with arguments $i, j$ to $(i, j)$ in the first copy of…
nodes.title: Regex nodes as a sum type

nodes.summary: For a natural number $k$ and a node $n$, the productions of node $k$ are the following encoded productions, all with left-hand side $k$, where nonterminal $i$ stands for node $i$: none if $n$ is the zero node; $k \to \varepsilon$ if $n$ is the empty-word node; $k \to a$ if $n$ is the character $a$; if $n$ is a sum with arguments $i$ and $j$, the unit production $k \to i$ when $i < k$ and the unit production…
nodes.title: Productions of a node

nodes.summary: For an encoded regular expression $e$ and a natural number $k$, the node of $e$ at index $k$ is the entry at position $k$ (counting from $0$) of its list of nodes, or the zero node when $k$ is at least the length of the list.
nodes.title: Node at an index

nodes.summary: For every encoded regular expression $e$, the number of Thompson states of $e$ computed by the pass over its nodes equals the Thompson state count of the regular expression that $e$ denotes.
nodes.title: The pass counts the states of Thompson's automaton

nodes.summary: The number of Thompson states of an encoded regular expression $e$ is the entry of the state counts of the nodes of $e$ at the last node, the root (read as $0$ when $e$ has no nodes).
nodes.title: Thompson state count of an encoding

nodes.summary: For triples of booleans $b = (b_1, b_2, b_3)$ and $c = (c_1, c_2, c_3)$, the flags of the sum are $(b_1 \lor c_1, b_2 \lor c_2, b_3 \lor c_3)$.
nodes.title: Flags of a sum

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $k$, $i$ and $j$, the productions of a sum node $k$ with arguments $i$ and $j$ are the unit production $k \to i$ if $i < k$, followed by the unit production $k \to j$ if $j < k$ (and nothing else). Nonterminals are node indices.
nodes.title: Productions of a sum node

nodes.summary: Over a primitively encodable finite alphabet with decidable equality and a fixed enumeration of its letters, the equivalence test, as a function of two encoded regular expressions, is primitive recursive.
nodes.title: The equivalence test is primitive recursive

nodes.summary: For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, the search bound $2^{m+n}$ for equivalence of two encoded regular expressions over $\alpha$, where $m$ and $n$ are the numbers of states of Thompson's automata of the two expressions, is a primitive recursive function of the pair of encoded expressions.
nodes.title: The equivalence search bound is primitive recursive

nodes.summary: For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, the number of states of Thompson's automaton of an encoded regular expression over $\alpha$, computed by one pass over its nodes, is a primitive recursive function of the encoding.
nodes.title: The Thompson state count of an encoding is primitive recursive

nodes.summary: For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, the map sending a list of regular-expression nodes over $\alpha$ to the list of their Thompson state counts, computed in one left-to-right pass, is primitive recursive.
nodes.title: The pass of Thompson state counts is primitive recursive

nodes.summary: For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, the map sending a list $c$ of natural numbers and a regular-expression node over $\alpha$ to the Thompson state count of the node computed from $c$ is primitive recursive.
nodes.title: One step of the Thompson state count is primitive recursive

nodes.summary: Let $l$ and $m$ be lists of regular-expression nodes and let $k$ be smaller than the length of $l$. Then the regular expression at node $k$ of the encoding with nodes $l$ followed by $m$ equals the regular expression at node $k$ of the encoding with nodes $l$.
nodes.title: Appending nodes does not change earlier expressions

nodes.summary: For an encoded regular expression $e$ and $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the regular expression at node $k$ is defined by recursion on $k$ from the node of $e$ at index $k$ (a zero node when $k$ is past the end): a zero node gives $0$, an epsilon node gives $1$, a node for a letter $a$ gives $a$, and a sum, product or star node gives the sum, product or star of the regular expressions at its arguments, where an argument that…
nodes.title: Regular expression at a node

nodes.summary: A node of an encoded regular expression over an alphabet $\alpha$ is one of six kinds: zero, epsilon, a letter $a \in \alpha$, a sum with arguments $i, j \in \mathbb{N}$, a product (concatenation) with arguments $i, j \in \mathbb{N}$, or a star with argument $i \in \mathbb{N}$, where the arguments are indices of nodes.
nodes.title: Regular-expression node

nodes.summary: Given a triple of Booleans $(b_1, b_2, b_3)$, the flags of its star are $(\mathrm{true}, b_2, b_2)$. Read as the flags (nonempty, has a nonempty word, infinite) of a language, a star is always nonempty, and it has a nonempty word, and is infinite, exactly when the argument has a nonempty word.
nodes.title: Flags of a star

nodes.summary: For natural numbers $k$ and $i$, the productions of a star node $k$ with argument $i$ are $k \to \varepsilon$, followed by $k \to i\,k$ if $i < k$ (and nothing else). Nonterminals are node indices.
nodes.title: Productions of a star node

nodes.summary: For every list $l$ of regular-expression nodes and every node $n$, let $l'$ be the list $l$ with $n$ appended at the end. Then the list of Thompson state counts of $l'$ is the list of counts of $l$ followed by one more entry, the count of $n$ computed from the counts of $l$.
nodes.title: Appending a node appends its count

nodes.summary: For a list $l$ of regular-expression nodes, the list of Thompson state counts of $l$ is computed in one left-to-right pass: starting from the empty list, each node $n$ of $l$ in turn appends the count of $n$ computed from the list of counts built so far.
nodes.title: Thompson state counts of a node list

nodes.summary: Given the list $A$ of flag triples of the nodes before it, the flag triple of a node is $(\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false})$ for a zero node, $(\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false})$ for an epsilon node and $(\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false})$ for a letter node. For a sum, product or star node it is the flags of a sum, product or star applied to the entries of $A$ at its…
nodes.title: Flags of the next node

nodes.summary: Let $c = (c_0, \dots, c_{m-1})$ be a list of natural numbers, and read $c_i$ as $0$ when $i \ge m$. The Thompson state count of a regular-expression node from $c$ is $0$ for the node $0$, $1$ for the node $\varepsilon$, $2$ for a letter, $c_i + c_j$ for a sum node and for a concatenation node with arguments $i$ and $j$, and $c_i + 1$ for a star node with argument $i$.
nodes.title: One step of the Thompson state count

nodes.summary: For an encoded regular expression $e$ and an encoded DFA $D$, the inclusion test returns the Boolean computed by the CFG ⊆ DFA inclusion test on the grammar of $e$ and the automaton $D$.
nodes.title: Inclusion test

nodes.summary: For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, the property of an encoded regular expression over $\alpha$ that the language it denotes is empty (E_REX) is decidable by a multi-stack machine.
nodes.title: Emptiness of regular expressions is decidable

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite alphabet with a primitive recursive encoding. Then equivalence of encoded regular expressions over $\alpha$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine: some multi-stack machine decides, for a pair $(e_1, e_2)$ of encoded regular expressions over $\alpha$, whether the regular expressions that $e_1$ and $e_2$ denote have the same language.
nodes.title: EQ_REX is decidable

nodes.summary: For an alphabet $\alpha$ with a primitive recursive encoding, the property of an encoded regular expression over $\alpha$ that the language it denotes is infinite is decidable by a multi-stack machine.
nodes.title: Infiniteness of regular expressions is decidable

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with decidable equality and a primitive recursive coding by natural numbers. The set of pairs $(e, D)$ of an encoded regular expression $e$ over $\alpha$ and an encoded DFA $D$ over $\alpha$ such that the language of the regular expression denoted by $e$ is contained in the language of $D$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine.
nodes.title: Inclusion of a regular language in a DFA language is decidable

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with a primitive recursive coding by natural numbers. The set of pairs $(e, w)$ of an encoded regular expression $e$ over $\alpha$ and a word $w$ over $\alpha$ such that $w$ belongs to the language of the regular expression denoted by $e$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine.
nodes.title: Membership for regular expressions is decidable

nodes.summary: For an encoded regular expression $e$ with $n$ nodes, its grammar is the encoded context-free grammar with start nonterminal $n - 1$ (truncated subtraction, so $0$ when $n = 0$), in which nonterminal $k$ stands for node $k$. Its productions are, for each node $k < n$: none if node $k$ is $0$; $k \to \varepsilon$ if it is $\varepsilon$; if it is the letter $a$, the production $k \to a$; if it is the sum of nodes $i$…
nodes.title: The grammar of an encoded regular expression

nodes.summary: For every regular expression $r$ over an alphabet $\alpha$, the encoded regular expression obtained by flattening $r$ (listing the nodes of its subexpressions in postorder, so that the root of $r$ is the last node) denotes $r$.
nodes.title: Every regular expression has an encoding

nodes.summary: An encoded regular expression $e$ with $n$ nodes denotes the regular expression at its node $n - 1$, the last node. For $n = 0$ this is the expression at node $0$, which lies past the end of the list and is the empty expression $0$.
nodes.title: The regular expression denoted by an encoding

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be an alphabet with decidable equality, $e$ an encoded regular expression over $\alpha$ and $k$ a natural number. Every word in the language of the regular expression at node $k$ of $e$ is yielded by the sentential form consisting of the single nonterminal $k$ in the context-free grammar of $e$.
nodes.title: Completeness of the grammar of an encoded regular expression

nodes.summary: The flag triple of the empty language is $(\mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false}, \mathrm{false})$; the three flags of a language say whether it is nonempty, whether it has a nonempty word, and whether it is infinite. This triple is also read for an argument of a node that is not an earlier node.
nodes.title: Flags of the empty language

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.

breadcrumbs.label: Decision procedures for automata, grammars and strings
